title: A deletion system can make requests contestable without publicly proving complete data control
source_unit: California Privacy Protection Agency official DROP consumer guidance, data-broker processing guidance, and July 2026 explainer
geography: California residents and data brokers participating in the Delete Request and Opt-out Platform

observations.period: January-August 2026 launch and initial processing framework

denominator.unit: official DROP workflow and processing-rule description, not a request-level outcome sample

reachable_data_brokers.unit: data brokers reachable through one DROP request

visible_status_categories.unit: deleted, exempted, opted out, record not found, and pending

maximum_initial_status_reporting_window.unit: days; time that status updates may take

aggregate_deletion_completion.value: not publicly reported on the official pages reviewed
aggregate_deletion_completion.unit: request-level completion, downstream deletion, and reappearance

observations.method: Review of California Privacy Protection Agency consumer and broker workflow pages; system features, legal timing, and status categories are kept separate from actual request outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: The public pages describe a newly operating process and do not provide an aggregate request ledger, broker-level completion rates, match rates, downstream contractor audits, residual copies, reappearance, consumer harm, or trust outcomes. Early statuses may be incomplete within the 90-day reporting window.
observations.subgroup: California residents submitting DROP requests and data brokers subject to California's accessible deletion mechanism; the system is not a national platform or a representative survey.
observations.counterinterpretation: A trackable request, recurring suppression duty, per-broker status, and ability to add identifiers may create real consumer leverage even without a public aggregate completion table. Lack of aggregate outcome data is a measurement boundary, not proof that the system fails.

denominator.unit: approximately California consumers registered for DROP; agency-reported milestone

profile_deleted_by_at_least_one_broker.unit: percent of consumers reported by CalPrivacy as having a profile deleted by at least one broker

typical_broker_deletion_reach.unit: more than 40 brokers for the typical DROP user

brokers_reporting_processing.unit: approximately percent of brokers reported as having processed deletion requests

all_broker_deletion_and_durable_control.unit: missing all-broker status distribution, permanent re-collection check, exemption validity, trust, switching, or wellbeing outcome

observations.method: Official California Privacy Protection Agency implementation follow-up; agency-reported typical-user and at-least-one-broker results are retained separately from the broker-level processing share and from verified all-broker deletion.
observations.uncertainty: The announcement does not publish the full consumer-broker status matrix, define the typical-user calculation in detail, show how many of the 654 brokers matched each person, verify deletion across every broker, establish exemption or not-found rates, or measure re-collection, trust, switching, or wellbeing.
observations.subgroup: California DROP registrants and participating data brokers; the 99.9% and typical-user figures are agency-reported aggregate implementation outcomes, not a person-level audit sample.
observations.counterinterpretation: Deletion by at least one broker and deletion from more than 40 brokers can represent meaningful reduction in exposure while leaving unmatched, exempted, pending, opted-out, or re-collected records at other brokers; implementation progress is not the same as complete privacy control.

related_sources.claim: Data brokers must process requests, report status, repeat the cycle at least every 45 days, and direct service providers or contractors to take the required action.
CalPrivacy describes the more-than-600-broker route and visible status categories.

boundary: This record measures the visibility and rules of California's DROP deletion process. It does not establish a deletion success rate, complete downstream control, broker compliance, reappearance, reduced harm, trust, wellbeing, or durable consumer exit.
